sources.title: BOAST: Diagnosis and Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Extremities

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Fractures (complex): assessment and management (NG37)

indications: Acute compartment syndrome of the leg diagnosed clinically, or by pressure measurement where clinical assessment is unreliable.
After revascularisation of an ischaemic limb, where fasciotomy must always be considered.
Prophylactically in selected high-risk injuries at the surgeon's judgement.
contraindications: Late presentation with established muscle death: discuss between two consultants, since non-operative management with renal protection may be safer.
preparation: The decision is an emergency (NCEPOD category 1); theatre is not delayed for further imaging.
Consent covers open wounds, a second look, skin grafting or flap closure, muscle loss and amputation risk.
Creatine kinase and renal function for baseline.
positioning: Supine, with the leg supported so both medial and lateral sides are accessible.
equipment: Major orthopaedic or general set, long scissors.
anatomy: Anterior compartment: tibialis anterior, toe extensors, anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve.
Lateral compartment: peronei and the superficial peroneal nerve, which pierces the fascia in the distal third.
Superficial posterior compartment: gastrocnemius and soleus.
Deep posterior compartment: tibialis posterior and long toe flexors, with the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve; reached by detaching soleus from the back of the tibia.
criticalSafety: Decompress all four compartments and confirm each one is open.
The deep posterior compartment is the one most often missed.
Long incisions. A short skin incision can still constrict the swollen muscle beneath it.
Document the viability of the muscle in each compartment.
structuresAtRisk: Posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve
commonErrors: Closing the skin at the first operation.
complications: Muscle necrosis and infection requiring further debridement.
Nerve injury, particularly the superficial peroneal nerve.
Chronic wound problems, skin graft requirement and altered appearance.
postop: Plastic surgery discussion within 24 hours and re-exploration within 72 hours, or earlier if indicated.
Creatine kinase, renal function and urine output monitoring.
Delayed primary closure, or split-thickness skin grafting when it cannot be closed.

steps.emphasis: Leg supported so both the medial and lateral aspects can be reached without moving it.
Apply but leave deflated: the muscle is already ischaemic and you need to see it bleed.
Excise only clearly dead muscle now. Doubtful muscle is reassessed at the planned second look.
Do not close the skin. Cover with a sealed or negative-pressure dressing and set the date for the second look.
Record each compartment and its muscle viability by name.

step.fas.lateral.title: Lateral incision: anterior and lateral compartments
step.fas.lateral.why: One lateral incision over the intermuscular septum releases both the anterior and the lateral compartments, provided the septum is found first.
how: Incise anterior to the fibula along the length of the leg.
Make a small transverse cut in the fascia to identify the anterior intermuscular septum.
Release the anterior compartment fascia in line with tibialis anterior and the lateral compartment fascia in line with the fibula, proximally and distally under direct vision.
structuresAtRisk: Superficial peroneal nerve in the distal third
pitfalls: Releasing only one of the two compartments because the septum was not identified.
Dividing the superficial peroneal nerve where it pierces the fascia.

step.fas.medial.title: Medial incision: superficial and deep posterior compartments
step.fas.medial.why: The deep posterior compartment is the one that is missed, and it contains the posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve.
how: Incise a short distance behind the posteromedial border of the tibia, protecting the saphenous vein and nerve.
Release the superficial posterior compartment fascia over gastrocnemius and soleus.
Detach soleus from the back of the tibia to enter and release the deep posterior compartment along its length.
structuresAtRisk: Posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve
